title: Groundwater in Punjab
body: Punjab's fertile plains were at the heart of the Green Revolution, which helped India become self-sufficient in food. From the 1960s, farmers shifted to high-yielding varieties of wheat and paddy. These new seeds needed more water than traditional seeds, so farmers began to pump groundwater for irrigation. Free power supply encouraged even more pumping. Modern farming also relied on chemical fertilisers and pesticides. Over time, the groundwater level in a large part of the state fell so low that water is not reached until depths of about 30 metres, and chemicals from fertilisers and pesticides dissolved in the groundwater, creating health hazards. Almost 80% of Punjab's area is now classified as 'over-exploited'. Food security was achieved for the short term, but healing the long-term damage will take time and effort. The problem is not limited to Punjab; many other states face it too.
